title: FDA GRAS reform: what foodservice operators should do now
summary: FDA's proposed GRAS rule targets ingredient makers, but multi-unit operators feel it next. See the timeline, state laws and supplier steps to take now.
body_markdown:
## Executive summary: what operators should know about GRAS reform


- FDA's August 2026 proposal would require companies to notify the agency when they make their own GRAS determinations, including determinations for food-contact materials like packaging and adhesives. Public comments close December 9, 2026.


- The scientific bar for GRAS stays the same, and the rule would not add approval before a product goes to market. What changes is how much FDA gets to see.


- Kevin C. Kenny of FoodChain ID expects a final rule in late 2027 at the earliest, with full compliance landing around 2029 or 2030. He still advises starting now, because the documentation takes longer to pull together than most companies expect.


- Restaurants and c-stores mostly won't file anything, but they'll absorb the effects through supplier questions, reformulated ingredients and substitutions that have to show up on every label at every location.


- The useful work for operators now is knowing which suppliers stand behind your proprietary ingredients, asking them for their regulatory basis, and making sure an ingredient change can reach every store quickly.


## What is GRAS, and why does FDA want to change it?


**GRAS stands for “generally recognized as safe.”** It’s a category that dates back to the 1958 Food Additives Amendment, **which lets ingredients that qualified experts widely agree are safe for a specific use skip the FDA approval process that food additives go through** . Salt, vinegar and baking soda all qualify, which is a good reminder that GRAS isn’t a list of mystery chemicals. It also covers thousands of newer ingredients, from fibers and proteins to flavor components and processing aids.


The sticking point has always been who makes that call, since a company can review the science, decide its ingredient is GRAS and start selling it without ever telling FDA. The agency has offered a voluntary notification program since the late 1990s, and plenty of companies use it, but nothing requires them to. Critics call that gap the “GRAS loophole,” and consumer advocates have pushed to close it since at least 2013. Speaking at[Food Safety Magazine’s October webinar on GRAS reform](https://www.food-safety.com/events/11585-fda-proposes-major-gras-reform-what-it-could-mean-for-your-business) , food regulatory attorney Kevin C. Kenny of FoodChain ID put the problem simply: some substances in the food supply are ones FDA doesn’t know are there, and it’s hard to keep an eye on something you don’t know exists.


## What the proposed rule would change


FDA published the[proposed rule on substances generally recognized as safe](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/11/2026-16296/substances-generally-recognized-as-safe) in the Federal Register on August 11, 2026. Its central change converts GRAS notification from voluntary to mandatory. Companies can still reach their own GRAS conclusions, but they would have to report them to FDA. The requirement covers direct food ingredients, food-contact substances and animal food.


What would change


What stays the same


Companies must tell FDA about GRAS decisions they make on their own The science behind what counts as GRAS


Self-affirmed ingredients already on the market get a shorter filing, with proof they were sold in the U.S. Ingredients FDA has already reviewed or listed in its regulations


An exemption for tiny trace amounts, once limited to packaging, extends to food ingredients No approval needed before launch, so products keep selling during FDA’s review


FDA publishes a public list of the shorter filings submissions


According to[Covington's analysis of the proposed GRAS rule](https://www.cov.com/en/news-and-insights/insights/2026/08/fda-issues-proposed-rule-on-substances-generally-recognized-as-safe-gras) , the rule runs on visibility more than penalties. Skipping a required notice wouldn’t automatically make a food illegal to sell, but it would move that ingredient up FDA’s list for a closer look. Lawyers are already arguing over whether FDA can require notices at all, since the 1958 law lets companies make GRAS calls without the agency.[Venable’s review of FDA’s GRAS rulemaking](https://www.venable.com/insights/publications/2026/07/new-details-emerge-on-fdas-gras-rulemaking) raises significant doubts about FDA’s authority to do it on its own, and several bills in Congress could settle the question.


Self-affirmed ingredients already in use get a shortcut, a streamlined filing instead of a full safety dossier. The catch, Kenny said, is proving the ingredient was actually sold in the U.S. for the use its GRAS conclusion covers. An invoice proves a sale happened, not what the ingredient went into, so purchase orders, shipping records and formulation histories end up doing the heavy lifting. A supplier that can’t produce them loses the shortcut and is back to a full dossier or a food additive petition.


## The timeline, and why the advice is to start now


[Comments on the proposed GRAS rule](https://www.regulations.gov/commenton/FDA-2025-N-3262-0001) are open until December 9, 2026, and every later date depends on when FDA finalizes it. Kenny doesn't expect a final rule before the fourth quarter of 2027 and thinks 2028 is more likely. Once the final rule is published, the clock runs in three steps:


- The rule takes effect 60 days after publication.


- Streamlined submissions for existing ingredients are due 12 months after the effective date.


- Full compliance is due 18 months after the effective date.


That would put full compliance in late 2029 or 2030. Kenny still urged companies to begin now, and told a story from the PFAS rollout to explain why. A friend of his had collected certifications from roughly 3,000 vendors stating their materials contained no PFAS. Within eight months, as state PFAS requirements took hold, about 1,000 of those vendors discovered they did, which is not the kind of update anyone wants to bring back to the CEO. He expects GRAS to produce the same kind of surprise, with suppliers learning late in the window that their documentation doesn't hold up.


He also expects a bottleneck at FDA, which has historically handled around 50 GRAS notices a year, had already received about 80 this year by late October, and could see thousands once the filing window opens. He thinks the 12-month window will need to stretch to 24 months or longer, partly because every company will be calling the same small pool of regulatory consultants and toxicologists at the same time.


## Why restaurant and c-store operators feel it second


The companies filing notices will be ingredient makers, flavor houses and packaging suppliers, so most foodservice operators will never send anything to FDA under this rule. They'll feel it through the supply chain in a few predictable ways.


**Some suppliers will reformulate or be replaced** if they can't document an ingredient's GRAS basis. Switching suppliers was one of the options FoodChain ID toxicologist Tom Jonaitis raised for that situation, which comes up again below. Either way, the sauce base, seasoning blend or dressing your locations rely on could change. Reformulation is already picking up for other reasons as well, since[FDA's revocation of Red No. 3 in food](https://www.fda.gov/food/food-ingredients-packaging/fda-encourages-food-manufacturers-accelerate-phasing-out-use-fdc-red-no-3-foods-2027-deadline) reaches its compliance date on January 15, 2027.


**International supply chains carry the most risk,** according to Kenny, who called overseas suppliers his single biggest concern and said many people he met at a recent conference in Europe were unaware the rule was coming. Brands expanding into the U.S. with signature sauces or ingredients sourced from their home markets are especially exposed, because a supplier may sign a compliance statement without understanding what U.S. documentation requires.


**Some operators are closer to manufacturing than they realize,** including chains running commissaries, c-stores building fresh and private-label programs, and brands developing proprietary ingredients with a co-packer. These companies may own more of the paperwork than they assume, so it's worth asking regulatory counsel where yours falls.


## State laws are moving faster than FDA


While the federal rule works its way through comments, several states aren’t waiting. New York’s[Food Safety and Chemical Disclosure Act (S1239)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/S1239) passed both chambers in April 2026. According to[Davis Wright Tremaine’s summary of the New York GRAS bill](https://www.dwt.com/insights/2026/06/new-york-gras-food-ingredient-disclosure-bill) , it would make it unlawful to sell or use a non-exempt GRAS substance in food unless a safety report is on file with the state and posted publicly, and it would ban Red No. 3, propylparaben and the dough conditioner potassium bromate. As of writing this, the governor hasn’t acted on it, and it would take effect 180 days after signing.[Venable’s analysis of who the New York bill affects](https://www.venable.com/insights/publications/2026/05/new-yorks-food-safety-and-chemical-disclosure-act) focuses on brands, ingredient suppliers and contract manufacturers, but whether it reaches foodservice is still an open question, so operators with New York locations should check with counsel.


Elsewhere,[Louisiana pushed its additive disclosure law back to December 31, 2028](https://www.mofo.com/resources/insights/260713-summer-so-far-key-food-regulatory-litigation-developments) ,[California’s version stalled in committee in May](https://www.foster.com/newsroom/legal-alerts/californias-food-additive-and-ingredient-disclosure-bill-stalls-but-scrutiny-continues/) , and[Pennsylvania and New Jersey had their own bills pending this summer](https://www.verdantlaw.com/gras-reform-update-where-do-things-stand/) . For a chain operating in a dozen states, that adds up to a patchwork of lists and deadlines. If that sounds familiar, it’s because[state allergen labeling laws such as New York’s](https://www.transact-tech.com/resources/blog/manual-food-labeling-allergen-compliance) took the same route.


## Packaging and labels are part of this too


The rule also reaches food-contact materials when their safety status rests on a GRAS determination. “Everything in your kitchen is a food contact application,” Kenny told the audience, from packaging and coatings to adhesives and equipment. Most of it is already covered by specific FDA regulations and won’t need anything new, but it’s worth asking vendors which rule covers what, including the labels on your containers. Label adhesives, for example, are typically covered by[21 CFR 175.105](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-175/subpart-B/section-175.105) , while the label paper and its coating need their own basis.


## What multi-unit operators can do now


Two audience questions at the end of the webinar came close to what multi-unit operators are asking, and the speakers' answers translate well to a chain's headquarters.


### How should a company with hundreds of ingredients decide where to start?


Kenny's answer was to inventory everything first, then sort it into three tiers by risk. High priority covers ingredients with limited documentation, older safety assessments, significant exposure, manufacturing changes or emerging toxicology concerns. He called these the "problem children" and said he'd focus all of his energy on them right now. Medium priority covers ingredients with a plausible GRAS basis but gaps in the paperwork or changes to the specification. Well-documented ingredients with a clear regulatory status can be set aside for now. A large chain's menu easily runs to hundreds of ingredients, so the same triage works for deciding which supplier conversations to have first.


### What if a supplier can't document an ingredient's GRAS status?


Jonaitis treated that as a red flag to escalate, with a third-party review where confidentiality is the obstacle, and said that if nothing is forthcoming the next step may be an alternate supplier. His reasoning is worth keeping in mind: "it's ultimately the company that puts it into the marketplace that is going to be at risk for additional scrutiny." For a restaurant or c-store brand, the name over the door carries that risk with guests, whoever turns out to be legally responsible.


### A six-step plan for headquarters


Most of this work sits with headquarters, purchasing and food safety leadership rather than individual stores, and none of it has to wait for the final rule.


1. **List the ingredients with real exposure.** Commodity staples are rarely the issue. Start with proprietary sauces, bases, seasoning blends, flavors and colors, plus anything sourced internationally.
2. **Ask suppliers for the regulatory basis of each one.** Good answers include a GRAS notice (GRN) number, a specific CFR citation or, for flavors, a FEMA GRAS listing. You can check any GRN a supplier gives you against FDA's[GRAS Notice Inventory](https://www.fda.gov/food/generally-recognized-safe-gras/gras-notice-inventory) . Jonaitis flagged several answers that need follow-up: a generic "covered by 21 CFR" with no section named, a GRN for an ingredient made from a different source or process, FEMA GRAS cited for a use or level outside its scope, and older GRAS conclusions with no updated review of the ingredient’s current specifications. Kenny said he and Jonaitis are reviewing conclusions as old as 1979, so this one is more common than it sounds.
3. **Sort the list into the three tiers above.** Work the high-priority ingredients first, and escalate any supplier that can't answer rather than waiting for the final rule.
4. **Write change notice into supplier specs and onboarding.** Ask suppliers to tell you before they reformulate, switch sources or change an ingredient's regulatory status, so a change doesn't first show up on the receiving dock. Chains adding regional distributors as they grow should make the same documentation request part of approving every new supplier.
5. **Decide how a change reaches every store.** When an ingredient changes, the recipe, allergen information and label need to update at every location together. Our guide to[recipe change management and ingredient labels](https://www.transact-tech.com/resources/blog/recipe-change-management-ingredient-labels) walks through that process, and the[food recall response playbook](https://www.transact-tech.com/resources/blog/food-recall-response-playbook) covers the faster version when a supplier issue turns urgent.
6. **Weigh in before December 9.** Operators can comment directly through regulations.gov or through trade groups such as the[National Restaurant Association](https://restaurant.org/) and[NACS](https://www.convenience.org/) .


*This article is general information, not legal advice. Talk with regulatory counsel about how the proposed rule and state laws apply to your operation.*

## Frequently asked questions


### What is GRAS reform?


GRAS reform refers to FDA's August 2026 proposed rule that would make GRAS notification mandatory. Companies could still decide on their own that an ingredient is generally recognized as safe, but they would have to notify FDA. The proposal also covers food-contact substances and animal food. Comments close December 9, 2026.


### Does the proposed GRAS rule apply to restaurants?


The federal rule is aimed at the companies that make and sell ingredients, flavors and food-contact materials, so most restaurants won't file notices. Operators will feel it through supplier reformulations and documentation requests. Chains that manufacture their own products, such as commissary or private-label items, should confirm their role with regulatory counsel.


### When will GRAS reform take effect?


It hasn't yet, because the rule is still a proposal. Regulatory experts at FoodChain ID expect a final rule in late 2027 at the earliest and more likely in 2028. It would take effect 60 days after publication, with streamlined filings due 12 months and full compliance 18 months after that.


### What is self-affirmed GRAS?


Self-affirmed GRAS, also called self-determined or independent GRAS, is when a company concludes on its own, often with an expert panel, that an ingredient is safe for its intended use and markets it without notifying FDA. The proposed rule would keep independent determinations but require companies to report them.


### Will GRAS reform ban ingredients?


The proposal doesn't ban anything on its own, and the scientific standard for GRAS stays the same. Ingredients could still leave the market indirectly if a supplier can't document their safety basis, or if FDA reviews a substance and concludes it no longer qualifies.


### What should operators do if a supplier can't document an ingredient's GRAS status?


Treat it as a red flag and escalate. Ask for the specific regulatory basis, consider a confidential third-party review if the supplier is protecting proprietary information, and line up an alternate supplier if nothing comes back. Plan for the recipe, allergen and label updates a supplier switch would require.


### What should I ask my suppliers about GRAS?


Ask for the regulatory basis of each proprietary ingredient: a GRAS notice number, a specific CFR citation or a FEMA GRAS listing for flavors. Ask whether any ingredient relies on a self-determination, whether they can document its current U.S. commercial use, and how the supplier will notify you of reformulations.
